items.title: offboard: delay-aligned INDI + corrected latency finding
items.body:
## Why

Follow-up to the S2 review. My shipped `docs/s2_latency_attribution.md` concluded INDI-offboard "needs a faster/lower-latency inner path (S3)." Reviewing that, an offline study shows the framing is imprecise — and the corrected finding is the part that transfers to the eventual **onboard** INDI in ArduPilot.

## What the offline study found

- The INDI increment `f_cmd = f_state + (a_cmd − g) − f_meas` cancels **only if `f_state` and `f_meas` refer to the same instant's thrust.** `f_state` was the command from *1 tick* ago; `f_meas` reflects the command realized ~(command-path latency) ticks ago → misaligned by the whole delay → `f_cmd` winds up.
- Sweeping a modelled command-path delay: plain INDI is stable to ~75 ms, winds up by ~110 ms, diverges past ~185 ms; **PD+ff is flat throughout.**
- **Delay-aligning `f_state` to the latency recovers INDI to PD+ff quality (0.10–0.15 m) at every latency tested.** Anti-windup / clamping does **not** help (bounds the runaway into ~2–3 m). Alignment tolerates under-estimating the latency, diverges if you over-estimate.

## Changes

- `OffboardGains.cmd_delay_ticks` (default **1** = unchanged behavior): ticks to delay the fed-back command so it aligns with the measured specific force. Bridge feeds `f_state` from a short ring buffer instead of "previous tick."
- New regression test `test_indi_needs_delay_alignment_under_latency` pinning: default INDI diverges under latency, aligned INDI recovers, PD+ff is robust.
- Corrected `docs/s2_latency_attribution.md`: de-synchronization (not irreducible latency); anti-windup is a red herring; **onboard implication** — match motor spin-up lag (~30 ms) + IMU filter delay before the increment, so low latency alone is not sufficient.

## Scope / caveats

Offline evidence only (fixed-delay model, instant attitude, no jitter) — **not VM-confirmed**, and the offboard delay buffer is throwaway scaffolding. Value is the corrected, transferable lesson for the onboard controller, backed by a test. S2's shipped flight config (PD+ff, 0.44–0.80 m) is unchanged. 81 tests pass.

items.title: Mandatory egress enforcement + on-demand secure sandbox runtime (mirror)
items.body:
Mirror of the enterprise egress-enforcement + sandbox work (LLD #63). Closes the network-security and runtime-isolation gap an audit found: the proxy **mediated** traffic but could not **deny** it, and nothing isolated the governed agent.

## What ships (defense in depth)
- **L1 — proxy egress policy** (`egress_policy.rs`, wired into `tls_mitm.rs`, `GET /intutic/egress`): `off`/`monitor`/`enforce`. In `enforce` the proxy denies (403, no tunnel) any destination not on its allow policy.
- **L2 — mandatory host firewall** (`firewall.rs` + `intutic enforce apply|remove|status|generate`): default-deny egress permitting only the proxy, DNS, established, and operator CIDRs.
- **L3 — container sandbox** (`intutic exec --sandbox`): `cap-drop=ALL`, `no-new-privileges`, read-only rootfs, resource caps, egress locked to the proxy. The agent ends with an empty capability set and cannot undo the firewall.
- **L4 — Firecracker microVM backend**: same interface, VM-grade boundary; `health()` refuses (never simulates) when KVM is absent.

## Verification
- L1: 12 unit tests + wired-handler integration test + real binary/curl + verify-by-neutralisation.
- L2: generated nftables ruleset applied in a privileged Linux container genuinely blocks direct egress; `--allow` opens exactly the named hole; 14 unit tests + neutralisation.
- L3: full `intutic exec --sandbox` end-to-end — user=sandbox, caps=[], proxy reachable, external blocked, firewall immutable.
- L4: microVM boots a guest kernel on real KVM (GCE nested-virt); honesty gate verified on a non-KVM host.
- Docs: overclaims corrected; latency-claims gate hardened (README + TeX) and the surfaced claims rewritten to architectural properties.
- CLI 195 tests · proxy egress/firewall/integration tests · typecheck · lint:claims · public-parity — all green.

**`benchmark.load` config block** (`mode: closed|open`, `rate`, k6-style `stages`, `max_in_flight` default 512, schema-ceiling 100000 enforced in the loader): default `closed` = zero behavior change for existing configs; closed mode strictly rejects open-mode knobs. Threaded `BenchmarkConfig → ResolvedServer → Suite`; JSON schema updated.

**Open-model scheduler** (`internal/client/loadgen.go`): piecewise-linear arrival-rate curve with an analytic inverse (constant segments divide; ramps solve the quadratic — exact arrival times, no drift). The arrival clock never blocks on workers: bounded queue full ⇒ counted `dropped_iterations` (k6 semantics). Single reused timer, single-goroutine counters.

**Measurement semantics**: CO-corrected response percentiles measured from *intended* send time (wrk2 semantics) lead in open mode (`OpenStats.Response`); service latency keeps the closed-loop-identical boundary (Do+read+close) for cross-mode comparability. Schedule-lag p50/p99/max (including window-canceled pickups — the longest-waiting tail), max backlog, target vs offered rate, attempted/dropped counts. `Stats.Rps` now computed in both modes. Transport pool sized off `max_in_flight` in open mode.

**Pre-existing export bug fixed** (surfaced by this PR's real-flow smoke, broken since the json/v2 migration): json/v2 has no default `time.Duration` representation, so `ExportServerResult` errored on the raw `SequenceStats` durations and silently dropped the whole per-server result file (exit 0). items.title: Fix latency_report duplicated day-rollup grain on mid-flow drop-off
items.body:
## Problem (C2)

`latency_report()` aggregates the per-segment frame at two grains and stacks them: an **hour pass** (`hour_local` 0–23) and a **day pass** (`hour_local = NA`). A segment whose prior-question timestamp is blank or unparseable — an ordinary non-responder / mid-flow drop-off — gets `NA` `segment_date_local`, and `hour_local` (derived from the same `batch_prior`) is `NA` too. So it already lands at the `(date=NA, hour_local=NA)` unknown-time bucket **in the hour pass**, and the day pass re-emits that identical key. The `rbind` then double-counts it.

Reproduced: one drop-off row → ~12 duplicate grain keys and an inflated `hour_local IS NULL` day partition (the downstream "day rollup" marker). The happy-path fixtures have no drop-offs, so the bug never surfaced in tests or on clean campaigns — it appears the moment a real campaign has a non-responder.

## Fix

Drop the hour pass's own `NA`-hour rows before stacking:

```r
hour_grain <- hour_grain[!is.na(hour_grain$hour_local), , drop = FALSE]
```

The `(hour=NULL)` unknown bucket belongs to the day partition only. The day pass reproduces every removed row (it forces `hour_local = NA` over the same frame, and `collapse_summary_to_day()` keeps NA-date groups), so this drops only duplicates — never unique data — and the diagnostic counts (`n_na_parse` etc.) survive exactly once instead of twice. The consolidated grain `(campaign_id, date, hour_local, segment, threshold_min)` is now unique.

## Tests (T1)

- New regression test asserts grain uniqueness (`anyDuplicated == 0`) on a fixture with a mid-flow drop-off, and that the drop-off still lands in the day-rollup partition exactly once (not dropped). Confirmed it **fails on the pre-fix code** (`anyDuplicated` = 61) and passes after.
- Updated the stale comment in the `n_na_parse` test that documented the old double-counting as expected.

`make verify`: tests pass, lint clean, 100% coverage (`latency_report.R` included). Happy path unchanged — `test-day_rollup_equivalence.R` stays green.

Ref: survey160r code-analysis backlog item **C2 + T1**.

items.title: fix(learn): stream-live-ops taught a wire shape /ws/ops never emits
items.body:
## Problem

The `/learn/stream-live-ops` tutorial destructured every message as a tuple:

```js
const [opType, opData] = item.op
```

`/ws/ops` has never emitted that shape. `api/endpoints/ws.py::_serialize` sends a flat object:

```json
{ "op_id": "82134935.0", "timestamp": "...", "op_type": "award", "body": { ... } }
```

So all three snippets in the guide threw `Cannot destructure ... item.op is undefined` for anyone who pasted them. This is our public developer documentation, so the first thing a new integrator tried didn't run.

## Fix

Rewritten against the actual endpoint:

- **Correct four-field shape** in all snippets.
- **Server-side filters documented** — `?op_type=` and `?account=` existed in `ws.py` but the guide never mentioned them, so readers were told to filter client-side over the full firehose.
- **Honest `?account=` caveat** — `ACCOUNT_FIELDS` in `helpers/pubsub.py` does not include an award's `initiator`, so `?account=alice` catches awards alice *received*, not ones she sent. Called out explicitly rather than letting readers discover it in production.
- **`op_id` → block number** — it's `<block>.<op-fraction>`; the integer part is the block. Same parse `web/lib/broadcast-confirm.ts` relies on.
- **Corrected latency** — "within ~5 blocks of the tip" → 1.5–4.5s (3s blocks + 1.5s `LIVE_POLL_INTERVAL`).
- **Added two caveats** the guide omitted: the feed carries real ops only (virtual ops are emitted at irreversibility and never appear), and these are head blocks, not irreversible ones.

## Not changed

`custom-app-data.tsx:44` also destructures `item.op` as a tuple — but that one reads `getAccountHistory`, raw node RPC, where the tuple **is** the correct shape. Verified and left alone. Its `streamOps` snippet already used `{ body, timestamp }` correctly.

## Verification

Claims checked against source, not memory: `api/endpoints/ws.py` (`_serialize`, `_build_filter`), `api/helpers/pubsub.py` (`ACCOUNT_FIELDS`), `api/parser/live_stream.py` (`POLL_INTERVAL`, head-block/real-ops-only docstring), `web/lib/broadcast-confirm.ts` (`blockNumFromOpId`).

Gates: **tsc 0 · vitest 99/99 · `next build` ok**. Docs-only change, no runtime code touched.

items.title: Retract the cross-client latency finding, corrected to the evidence
items.body:
Supersedes the un-pushed local branch `docs/retract-latency-finding`, which a
peer session wrote and explicitly left "to merge, rewrite or bin". This is the
rewrite; their branch is untouched.

## Why a rewrite rather than a merge

The retraction was written before its author found the root cause, and it
asserted two things measurement here does not support.

**It named pinning as an amplifier.** "Pins every role to a single physical
core, which turns each extra scheduling hop into a full quantum." Tested here
under that harness's own publisher pinning (`taskset -c 0,4` — the two
hyperthreads of one physical core) and, as it turns out, against that harness's
own containerised broker: **1.18x pinned against 1.13x unpinned**, with the
four-point breakdown unchanged at 45 us to the wire and 26 us to settle. The
hop did not become a quantum. Its author independently withdrew the hypothesis.

**It attributed the whole calibration gap to the adapter.** My 17.7k is a tight
in-process loop with no pacer and no per-message bookkeeping — a ceiling, not a
like-for-like against a calibrator. The environment accounts for none of the gap
(≈17,960 under their broker and their pinning), which is worth recording, but
that is a measurement, not the conclusion the text drew.

**And it missed the root cause,** which its author found afterwards: the harness
paced each client at a fraction of its *own* calibrated capacity, so a faster
client was offered a higher absolute rate and sat further along its own
latency-versus-load curve. Reading that table across clients penalises whichever
client has the most headroom — MQTTium. That is the whole of the 2.95x, and it
is a method error rather than a defect on either side. They have since added a
fixed-rate scenario for cross-client comparison.

## What the corrected entry now records

- The root cause, named as a method error.
- The one quantified contributing cause: their adapter suspends a coroutine for
  the whole round trip on MQTTium while correlating gmqtt's ack in a callback,
  worth 11-34% growing with load. Reverted there rather than kept.
- The in-repo measurement: 1.18x pinned / 1.13x unpinned at 6,246 msgs/s, 71 us
  of library inside a 207 us round trip.
- That the same figures hold on the **`v1.0.0rc1` tag** that was measured
  externally, since the first objection to any of this is "you measured a build
  that had already been fixed". It had not been.
- Two hypotheses tested here that did **not** hold, recorded so nobody re-runs
  them: single-core pinning, and the knee later reported between 2,500 and
  5,000 msgs/s — which does not reproduce (0.270-0.284 ms against 0.251-0.301 ms
  over six alternated samples per point, on both the awaited and
  `publish_nowait` paths).
- The calibration question as open rather than answered.

## Convention

`docs/reports/` entries are records of what was believed on their date and are
never edited to match new findings; corrections live in the index. This follows
that, and the index already carried a correction for the same audit's other
conclusion.

## Verification

Documentation only. `tests/unit/test_documentation.py` passes.

Measurements behind it: alternated ABBA, three rounds, against
`eclipse-mosquitto:2.0.20` pinned to cores 1,5 with host networking — the same
broker instance the external campaign used, which was still bound to :11883.

items.title: Improve security, correctness, and docs (no dependency upgrades)
items.body:
Same treatment as the three Postgres repos, applied to the Mongo one. No library versions changed; still a small clone-and-run demo.

Correctness:
* server.js imported body-parser, which isn't a declared dependency (it only resolved transitively via Express). Switched to `express.json()` / `express.urlencoded()`.
* A bad `?limit` (e.g. `?limit=hello`) used to return the whole collection, because the number helper returned `''` and `.limit('')` let Mongoose return everything. It now falls back to the default (40).
* `connect()` never returned the `mongoose.connect` promise, so `await connect()` in `start()` resolved before the DB was reachable and a connection failure never reached the try/catch. It returns the promise now, so the await is meaningful.
* getUsers returned 400 on a DB/internal error; that's a 500 (still bodyless, nothing leaks).

items.title: deps: bump moonlight-common-c and adapt to the µs timing API
items.body:
Moves `core/moonlight-common-c` from `c86e0537` to `e41355ea` — 40 commits, clean fast-forward, no divergence — and adapts the two call sites that the API change breaks.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Not built, not tested.** I have neither a webOS toolchain nor a streaming host available, so neither the armv7 build nor the corrected latency readout has been exercised. Both need to pass before this merges. Everything below is static verification against the pinned sources.

## Why

In rough order of value for this project:

- **Reed-Solomon FEC decoding now goes through `nanors` with SIMD**, including an explicit path for non-x86 targets. FEC runs per packet on the inbound video stream, so this is the kind of work that matters on the ARM SoCs webOS TVs use. This is the main reason to take the bump.
- The ENet mutex is no longer taken to query RTT, and mouse/gamepad batching locking was reworked — less contention on the network and input paths.
- Thread context and `pthread_attr` leaks fixed.
- RTSP handling hardened against malformed `Session` headers and oversized responses.
- CMake max version specified for cmake-4.0 support.

## The API break, and the trap in it

`DECODE_UNIT` renamed two fields this codebase consumes and switched them from milliseconds to microseconds:

```
receiveTimeMs -> receiveTimeUs
enqueueTimeMs -> enqueueTimeUs
```

The rename alone is a compile error, which is the easy part. The trap is that `session_video.c` computed submit time as `LiGetMillis() - decodeUnit->enqueueTimeMs`. A mechanical rename leaves **milliseconds minus microseconds** — it still compiles, it is silently 1000× off, and it feeds the `avg N ms` video latency readout in the stats overlay.

Upstream added `LiGetMicroseconds()` for exactly this. The accumulators now stay in microseconds end to end and the conversion happens once at display time, mirroring how `avgDecoderLatency` already handles its `latencyUs` input. `VIDEO_STATS` fields are renamed to carry the unit in the name (`totalSubmitTimeUs`, `totalReassemblyTimeUs`) so the next reader doesn't have to guess.

One side effect worth expecting: the video latency figure previously accumulated whole milliseconds per frame and truncated, so sub-millisecond submit times displayed as `0.00`. It will now show real values. That is a correction, not a regression, but the number on screen will change.

## What was verified statically

- `STREAM_CONFIGURATION` and all three callback structs are **byte-identical** to the pinned version.
- All **20 `Li*` symbols** this codebase calls still exist, with unchanged signatures.
- A repo-wide grep confirms the two renamed fields are the entire breaking surface — nothing outside `src/`, including `core/libgamestream`, touches them.
- All **7 CI checkouts** use `submodules: recursive` and both `easy_build.sh` scripts use `--init --recursive`, so the new nested `nanors` submodule is fetched everywhere. No workflow change needed.
- The new `cmake_minimum_required(3.1...4.0)` and `C_STANDARD 11` are compatible with this repo's root `3.19`.

## For reviewers

**The unproven part is the build.** `moonlight-common-c` gains a nested submodule (`nanors`) whose sources — including `deps/obl/oblas_*.c` — are compiled directly, with SIMD dispatched internally and no architecture conditionals in its CMake. This is the first time that path is built for `arm-webos-linux-gnueabi` here. CI is the fastest way to answer it.

The second commit only adds a comment. `Limelight.h` now states that `LiGetMicroseconds()` "should only ever be compared with the return value from a previous call to itself", and it dropped the old explicit guarantee that `enqueueTime` shares that epoch. The subtraction is correct today — `VideoDepacketizer.c` sets `enqueueTimeUs = PltGetMicroseconds()` and `Misc.c` defines `LiGetMicroseconds()` as a passthrough to the same clock — but nothing in the API promises it stays that way, and a future mismatch would underflow into a truncated garbage latency with no compile error. The comment records that so the next bump re-checks it.

Two pre-existing issues were found in the touched functions and deliberately left alone, both worth a separate PR:

- `totalCaptureLatency` accumulates per *received* frame ([session_video.c:175](https://github.com/mariotaku/moonlight-tv/blob/main/src/app/stream/video/session_video.c#L175)) but is divided by `submittedFrames` at display, so the host-latency average inflates whenever SS4S rejects frames — i.e. exactly when the stream is struggling.
- `totalReassemblyTimeUs` is written every frame and never read anywhere.

items.title: Docs: Mermaid architecture diagrams, corrected layer counts and latency guidance
items.body:
Follow-up to #1, which merged before this commit was pushed. Documentation only — no runtime code changes.

## Diagrams

The architecture doc led with a hand-drawn box-and-arrow diagram. It did not survive narrow viewports, and it could not be edited without redrawing the whole thing by hand. Replaced with **three Mermaid diagrams**, which GitHub renders natively:

| Diagram | What it makes visible |
|---|---|
| **System architecture** (`flowchart`) | The three processes, the shared `RLock` blackboard, and — the part the ASCII version buried — *which edges fire every timestep versus once per control interval*. |
| **One control interval** (`sequenceDiagram`) | That the solver is **stopped** for the width of the `Agent.decide()` bar, and the `alt` branch that bounds it. This is the clearest statement of the real-time constraint anywhere in the docs. |
| **Safety envelope** (`flowchart`) | The five stages between an LLM token and an actuator, including the rejection path back to the model. |

**Verified before committing**, rather than assumed: all three were parsed and rendered to SVG under Mermaid 11 (the major version GitHub uses) — 3 blocks, 3 SVGs, zero parse errors.

Two rendering hazards were found that way and fixed:
- Double quotes inside `sequenceDiagram` message text (parser risk) — removed.
- `classDef` used 8-digit `#RRGGBBAA` fills. Beyond patchy support, a fixed light fill is unreadable on GitHub's **dark** theme. Now stroke-only, so the diagrams stay legible in both themes.

## Two stale claims corrected

Adding the diagrams surfaced places where the prose contradicted itself and the code:

1. **Layer counts were wrong in two sections.** "Three layers keep that bounded" sat above a list of **five**. The safety section likewise claimed three stages when the code now has five — `seasonal_park()` and `_update_zone_trims()` were added during tuning and never documented. Both sections now match the implementation, with a table explaining what each stage guarantees and why the ordering matters.

2. **The latency section recommended something our own measurements contradict.** It suggested a quantised 8B model "comfortably clears a 15-25s turn budget". On 4 GB VRAM, `llama3.1:8b` (5.6 GB resident) is split 25 % GPU / 75 % CPU and takes **~18 s per tool call**, which is why this project runs a 3B model at ~4.5 s. §6 already documented that measurement, so the two sections disagreed with each other. The section now states the VRAM-fit finding.

## README

Added a **requirements-coverage table** mapping each stated core requirement to the module that implements it, so a reader can confirm coverage without reading the source. Also states plainly which deliverables live in the repo and which are submitted separately.

## Reviewer notes

- No changes under `eco_loop/`, `main.py`, or `dashboard.py` — `ARCHITECTURE.md` and `README.md` only.
- The diagrams are the main thing to look at; they are best reviewed in GitHub's rendered view rather than the diff.

And bounding thinking does **not** make `max_output_tokens` safe: with default thinking, caps of 256/384/1024 all returned `finish_reason=MAX_TOKENS` with empty text (hidden thinking consumes the budget), and the capped native-schema configs still intermittently wrote to the output ceiling. Production therefore runs **uncapped behind per-route timeouts** (45 s tools · 60 s text · 75 s image).

**Explicitly not measured (each needs live calls — quota approval pending):** (1) model-list enumeration for this key — the one 1b step never run; (2) other Gemma 4 variants (E2B/E4B/12B/31B) via the hosted API with this key; (3) audio input on any hosted variant; (4) long-context behaviour; (5) Interactions API behaviour for this model; (6) batch/caching endpoints.

items.title: docs: select primary Pi 5 camera (ADR-011) and correct camera assumptions
items.body:
## What this is

A purchasing decision plus the documentation to back it. **No code changes** — the hardware does not exist yet, and CLAUDE.md §4 says never assume hardware state.

## The reframing

The question was "which supplementary camera should I buy". Investigation says it isn't supplementary: **the Pi 5 has never had a camera attached.** Every frame the project has captured came from the OV5647 on the Pi 3B, either as a recorded clip (TRK-031) or over the CAM-002 MJPEG relay. So this is the *primary v0.3 tracking camera* — which keeps it inside v0.3 scope (`CLAUDE.md:36`, "one camera") rather than triggering Phase 3.

## The recommendation

**Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide NoIR (SC0875, IMX708)** + a 22-pin-to-15-pin Pi 5 camera cable + a mount. ~£50 total.

Chosen over the Global Shutter Camera because CM3 is NoIR natively, where the GS camera's IR filter can only be made IR-transmitting by permanent, warranty-voiding removal — an irreversible modification made before any IR signal has been measured. Chosen over CM3 Standard on coverage: 66° H cannot see the ADR-010 working area from the stated mount pose, which is the failure the current rig already exhibits.

Two non-obvious points in the decision:

- **Select the 1536×864 mode but deliver at 60 fps.** Rolling-shutter skew tracks *readout* time, not frame period, so picking the 120 fps-capable mode and extending vertical blanking roughly halves R-03 skew (~8.3 ms vs 16.6 ms) at no CPU cost and with no code.
- **Frames become `CV_8UC1`.** `ball_detector.cpp:35`, `calibration_marker_detector.cpp:65,84` and `frame_quality.cpp:42` each open with `cvtColor(..., COLOR_BGR2GRAY)`. Nothing reads a colour channel, and ADR-005 already rejects colour detection. Taking the YUV420 Y plane straight through deletes a debayer and three conversions per frame.

## Two factual corrections

- `CAM-001:25` justified the Pi 3B sensor node with *"CSI cable reach (15cm) prevents multi-camera on a single Pi 5"*. That is wrong — 15 cm is the cable in the box. Raspberry Pi sells shielded 22-pin cables to 500 mm; CSI-over-HDMI extenders reach metres. CAM-001 survives as coverage work, but its case needs re-arguing on coverage geometry rather than cable reach.
- The measured CAM-002 ceiling (720p15, ~6.6 Mbit/s, ~50 ms freshness) rules a networked node out of the hot path against a 60 fps / 30 ms median budget. The Pi 3B is reclassified as the recording/replay rig it has actually been.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `docs/adr/ADR-011-...md` | **New.** Camera selection + libcamera acquisition + `CV_8UC1` contract + 850 nm IR. Status `Proposed` with six measurement gates. |
| `docs/adr/README.md` | Index row |
| `docs/agent-reference/agent-reference.md` | Camera/CSI hardware facts; R-03 and R-05 rewritten; D-03 widened; D-07 added |
| `docs/tickets/CAM-001-...md` | Cable-reach premise struck through and corrected; latency evidence recorded |
| `docs/tickets/TRK-009b-...md` | Per-row temporal alignment added as the R-03 closure, with a falsification test |
| `docs/tickets/TRK-032/033/034` | **New.** libcamera FrameSource (design); greyscale migration (small); IMX708 bring-up (small) |
| `README.md`, `BOARD.md` | Subsystem table and board rows |

`python tools/board/board_check.py` → OK (51 board tickets, 64 story files).

## Why the ADR is `Proposed`, not `Accepted`

Everything it asserts about the IMX708 — the readout time, the coverage, the frame-rate behaviour — is reasoned from published specs, not measured on target. Gates G1–G6 in the ADR are the measurements that make it `Accepted`; TRK-034 is the ticket that takes them. The 850 nm choice in particular is a judgement call with no quantum-efficiency curve behind it, and is flagged as such in the ADR's Risks.

## Review focus

- Whether the escalation trigger is right: if gate G4 shows a correlation gap that per-row alignment can't close, the answer is the Global Shutter Camera. Is that the trade you want, given it means the IR-filter surgery?
- 850 nm vs 940 nm — this is coupled to the laser purchase and is the least-evidenced decision here.
- Whether `CV_8UC1` should land as one change (TRK-033) or be split.

Unrelated observation, not touched: `BOARD.md` marks TRK-014..021 and VIEW-002/003 done as of 2026-07-18, while `CLAUDE.md:29-35` still lists them as "not yet built". One of the two is stale.

items.title: [perf] Calibrate the gather thread knee via autotune instead of a fixed cap
items.body:
## Summary
Follow-up to the merged `MAX_PARALLEL_THREADS` knee-cap. Remove that
compile-time ceiling (it is inert under the default config and duplicates the
runtime, per-hardware cap) and instead fix the autotuner so the *existing* cap
mechanism picks the right saturation knee.

## Motivation
`resolve_thread_count` already clamps to the caller cap. The cap defaults to
`min(_GATHER_THREAD_CEILING=8, physical_cores/2)` = 8 on the EPYC 7763, and
`autotune.calibrate()` refines it over candidates `(1,2,4,8,16)` with
interleaved A/B rounds, knee selection, and per-fingerprint caching. So the
ceiling is already a runtime, calibrated, per-hardware value; the merged
`constexpr` (16) never binds under defaults (8 < 16) and only clamps explicit
caps above 16.

The one real gap: a size x thread sweep showed the knee is size-dependent —
~4 threads at 4M indices, ~8 at 16M, ~16 at >= 64M — but calibration ran at
`_CALIB_N_INDICES = 4_000_000`, below where the knee the cap governs appears.
Calibrating at 32M samples the saturated regime, so `_pick_knee` reflects
production-scale gathers.

## Changes
- `include/colstore/gather.hpp`: remove `MAX_PARALLEL_THREADS`.
- `src/cpp/gather.cpp`: remove the `by_work` clamp; keep the corrected
  latency-bound comments, now attributing the binding limit to the cap /
  `colstore.autotune` rather than the constant; neutralize a stale
  "bandwidth-bound" line.
- `tests/test_threading.py`: drop the ceiling assertions and mirror constant
  added by the prior PR (the cap, not a constant, governs the bound).
- `src/colstore/autotune.py`: `_CALIB_N_INDICES` 4M -> 32M, with rationale.

items.title: fix(engines): capture vLLM V1 per-request latency under profiling
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes audit finding 3 (`.product/research/f3f4-field-audit-2026-07-16.md`): vLLM
per-request latency never populated. Empirically the v0.11.0 exit sweep showed
`e2e_latency_samples: 0` and `latency_stats: null` on both vLLM cells.

Root cause (live-diagnosed in-container at vLLM 0.19.1, both `disable_log_stats`
settings):

- `engines/_observed.py` read the vLLM **V0** `RequestOutput.metrics` surface
  (`arrival_time` / `finished_time` / `first_token_time`). At **V1** that
  namespace no longer exists.
- The offline `LLM` entrypoint forces `disable_log_stats=True`
  (`vllm/entrypoints/llm.py:272-273`), so `RequestOutput.metrics` is `None` on
  the default path (`log_stats` gate at `v1/engine/output_processor.py:176`).
- When stats are enabled, `metrics` is a `vllm.v1.metrics.stats.RequestStateStats`
  carrying `first_token_latency` (wall-clock TTFT), `first_token_ts` /
  `last_token_ts` (engine-core **monotonic**, a different clock from
  `arrival_time`) and `num_generation_tokens`.

## Fix

A mechanism exists, so it is wired in (opt-in, mirroring the tensorrt
`return_perf_metrics` gate; `log_stats` adds per-iteration aggregation + logger
overhead, so it must not touch default energy runs):

- `_build_llm_kwargs` sets `disable_log_stats=False` only when
  `measurement.latency_profiling` is enabled.
- New plugin-local `_extract_request_stats` reads `RequestStateStats`: TTFT =
  `first_token_latency`; E2E = TTFT + monotonic decode interval
  (`last_token_ts - first_token_ts`); decode-average ITL over the longest
  output's tokens. The two clocks are never cross-subtracted.
- Mode is `proportional` (the ITL is a decode-average estimate); the
  `latency_profiling_unsupported` degradation flag still fires if profiling is
  requested but the engine returns nothing.
- The stale vLLM-only extractors are removed from `_observed.py` (their "shared
  with TRT-LLM" docstring was false; TRT-LLM uses its own `_extract_metrics_dict`).
- Latency docs corrected: vLLM latency is profiling-only, not always-on/free.

Default energy runs are unchanged (no `disable_log_stats` kwarg, empty lists,
mode `None`).

## Test plan

- Unit tests rewritten for the V1 `RequestStateStats` shape
  (`test_extended_capture.py`, `test_latency_profiling.py`).
- `make lint`, `make typecheck` clean; `make test` = 3044 passed, 36 skipped.
- **Live-verified through the real plugin path** (`VLLMEngine._build_llm_kwargs`
  -> `load_model` -> `run_inference`) in the `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.19.1`
  container on `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`:
  - profiling **off**: no `disable_log_stats` kwarg, `per_request_latencies_ms`
    / `ttft_ms` / `itl_ms` all empty, mode `None`.
  - profiling **on**: `disable_log_stats=False`; `ttft_ms=[507, 500]`,
    `per_request_latencies_ms=[982, 954]`, `itl_ms=[68, 65]` ms, mode
    `proportional` (internally consistent: E2E approx TTFT + 7 x ITL).

## Doc audit

`docs/reference/results-schema.md` and `docs/reference/library/ExperimentResult.md`
updated to state vLLM latency is profiling-only.

items.title: Standardise on ERA5 as the project's single reanalysis (over CERRA)
items.body:
## What

Adopts **ERA5** as the project's single reanalysis, replacing **CERRA** across the roadmap for every reanalysis role — pre-training, capacity-estimation weather, and the weather-abnormality climatology (from PR #366). CERRA stays documented in the data-sources list, with its corrected coverage/latency findings, but is marked **deprioritised**.

## Why

Checking CERRA's current coverage (prompted by PR #366) turned up that its 2025 "timely updates" extension now runs it from **1984 to present** — but only **~3.5 months behind real time**. That latency is too stale for the **near-real-time** weather that capacity estimation requires.

**ERA5** clears that bar and is a better fit overall:

- **ERA5T** near-real-time stream is **~5 days behind real time** (final ERA5 follows ~2–3 months later after QC).
- Covers **1940→present**, so it reaches even further back than CERRA for pre-training on the long power histories that predate the ENS archive (2024-04-01).
- Shares the ECMWF **IFS lineage** with our ENS forecasts, so systematic biases largely cancel when reanalysis and forecast are combined (pre-training domain shift; climatology anomaly z-scores).
- Lets us ingest **one** reanalysis instead of two.

**Trade-off:** ERA5 is 31 km vs CERRA's 5.5 km. That mostly matters for near-surface wind over complex terrain; softened by CM SAF SARAH-3 (0.05°) already supplying the high-resolution solar irradiance, and by the flat trial area. CERRA is kept in the list so it can be revisited as a targeted add-on if fine-scale wind ever proves decisive.

- `data-sources.md` — new canonical **ERA5** row; **CERRA** reframed as 🔬 deprioritised (keeping the corrected 1984→present / ~3.5-month-latency findings).

items.title: Fix headless ADM playout drift below 100 Hz
items.body:
PlayThreadProcess/CaptureThreadProcess paced with a stateless relative sleep (SleepMs(10 - work)) that compensates for work time but not the sleep's own wake-up latency, and re-anchored the reference to the wall clock each tick. Wake-up overhead (~1.5 ms on Linux, more under virtualization) therefore accumulated into the frame period, so playout pulled at ~87 Hz instead of 100 Hz and NetEq dropped ~13% of inbound audio to bound latency.

Sleep to an absolute 10 ms grid advanced by a fixed +10 each tick so latency is corrected against the deadline instead of accumulating, with a resync guard to avoid frame bursts after a long stall.

Fixes #243

items.title: fix(compliance): the regulator-facing report read three fields the journal never writes
items.body:
Found while working the next reader in Phase 1c. The migration is the smaller half of this PR.

## The report tells a regulator the gateway blocked nothing

`_aggregate_logs()` counted correctly — over keys that do not exist. `dict.get()` returns a default rather than raising, so instead of failing it produced confident zeros:

| read | actual journal key | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `verdict` | `risk_level` | `blocked` always 0 — and `allowed = total - blocked`, so the report claimed **100% of traffic was allowed** |
| `latency_ms` | `elapsed_ms` | `avg_ms` always 0.0 |
| `"INJECTION"` (upper) | flags are lower-case (`prompt_injection`) | `inj_hits` always 0 |

Measured against **3 377 production entries**, 30-day window, 2026-08-08:

| | reported | truth |
|---|---:|---:|
| total | 3377 | 3377 ✓ |
| blocked | **0** | 3100 |
| allowed | **3377** | 277 |
| injection hits | **0** | 3100 |
| avg latency | **0.0** | 652.4 ms |

The GDPR/ROPA report describes a gateway that blocked nothing, saw no injection attempts, and answered instantly — and offers that as evidence of compliance. Every figure was individually plausible, which is why it survived. `pii_hits` and the category breakdown were already correct, which made the rest look trustworthy.

## Fix

Against `build_entry()`, which is the authority on these names. `blocked` keeps its original meaning — HIGH **or** BLOCK severity, not `not allowed`: a permitted HIGH-risk request still counts, which is what the report's own text describes.

## And the 1c migration

Worth more here than elsewhere: the scan was **unwindowed** — `load_entries()` with no `days`, filtered in Python afterwards — so a request-path endpoint re-parsed the entire journal on every call. `events_store.compliance_report_stats()` answers in two grouped queries; the journal scan stays as the fallback and is now windowed.

## Tests

Nine. Beyond the corrected numbers, two guards for the *class* of bug rather than the instance:

- `_aggregate_logs` reads no key `build_entry` does not write
- `build_entry` still writes the names this module depends on — so a rename fails here instead of in a report

Plus: the scan is windowed, the mirror is preferred when it answers, and a mirror exception falls back to the journal.

ruff + mypy clean · 102 tests across compliance, posture, dashboard-mirror, `events_store` and journal-bound · five ratchets green.

## Note on `analytics/dashboard.py`

It was the next name on the 1c list and I did not migrate it — deliberately. It is a Streamlit page that builds a pandas DataFrame and performs ~26 row-level operations on it (10min/hour/day groupbys, flag and secret explosions, a raw event table). It needs rows, not aggregates, and it is operator-facing behind auth rather than a request path. Migrating it means rewriting the page as ~10 aggregate queries for no throughput benefit. Recommend recording that as a decision in §8 rather than leaving it open.

## Summary
- Replaces v0.1.12's single-sample serverOffsetMs with proper NTP-style clock sync.
- Captures t1 (local before request), t3 (serverNowMs), t4 (local after response) on every /api/state.
- Offset = (t3 + RTT/2) - t4, removing the one-way response transit that previously got charged to clock skew.
- Rolling window of 8 samples; canonical offset = smallest-RTT sample (classic NTP best-of-N).
- Server-side: no changes - /api/state already emitted serverNowMs.
- New log line `Clock sync - offset=. best-rtt=. samples=.` per change so RTT issues are visible.

Closes the ~1 second residual drift seen on v0.1.12 where two tablets on different network paths landed on different offsets.

items.title: fix(timer): make timed-mode countdown immune to a wrong device clock
items.body:
**What** — Timed daily, gauntlet, experimental, and free play measured elapsed time as `Date.now() - startedAt`, mixing the device clock against a server-stamped start; a phone whose clock ran ahead of real time started the countdown partly drained, expired early, and fired an early `POST /end` that finalized the session short of its allotted time.

**Why** — Server responses now include `server_now`, so the client samples a server-minus-device offset on receipt and rebases `startedAt` into device-clock terms; every later `Date.now()` read then cancels the device's absolute error, fixing `useTimer`, `TimerBar`, and `OverflowTimerBar` at once. This mirrors the RTT-probe offset multiplayer already applies (multiplayer is untouched). The math lives in a new pure `client/src/shared/timing/serverClock` module with tests that reproduce the reported bug (a 90s-fast phone) and verify skew immunity.

**Follow-ups** — One-way network latency is not corrected (biases the offset by tens of ms, always in the player's favor); acceptable for a 120–180s budget. Timer rendering wasn't verified live since the fix only diverges under a wrong device clock, which the browser tooling can't simulate — the pipeline unit tests are the verification.

## Summary

While auditing the SH-4 FPU coverage in `docs/insns.json`, the divide/square-root latencies were found to be wrong by roughly an order of magnitude — they recorded the *"1 issue cycle"* note from the manual instead of the actual result latency.

Corrected against **Table 8.3 of the SH7750 Hardware Manual (Rev 2.0)** (the Dreamcast SH-4 reference). Latency = first number of the manual's `L1/L2` pair:

| Instruction | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `fdiv FRm,FRn` (single) | 1 | **12** |
| `fsqrt FRn` (single) | 1 | **11** |
| `fdiv DRm,DRn` (double) | 2 | **24** |
| `fsqrt DRn` (double) | 2 | **23** |
| `lds.l @Rm+,FPSCR` | 3 | **4** |

The `.issue` fields were already correct (all `1`); only `.latency` changed. Five lines, values only — no structural change.

## Notes / not changed
- **No SH-4 instructions are missing.** The matrix/vector helpers (`ftrv`, `fipr`, `fmac`, XD-register `fmov`) are all present and correctly flagged; the JSON's 234 `SH4=true` rows match Table 8.3.
- `fsrra`/`fsca` remain flagged SH4A-only, matching the SH7750 manual (which never mentions them). The Dreamcast SH7091 silicon does implement them, so if the `SH4` column is meant as "Dreamcast-capable" that's a separate follow-up.
- The schema has only `issue`/`latency`, so it can't capture the F3 pipe-lock/pitch (10/9/23/22) that makes these ops expensive back-to-back.

items.title: perf(net): read COMPACT by offset — the span control arm stops building a tree
items.body:
Judged in an agent workflow (12 agents: 3 independent allocation probes, adversarial verification, ruling). All three probes reproduced the ledger independently and agreed exactly.

## Measured

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| terminus delivery | 202 ns | **~110 ns** (−46%) |
| terminus allocations | 11 | **3** |
| terminus bytes/frame | 735 | **212** |
| forwarding hop | 180 ns | **~90 ns** (−50%) |
| forwarding allocations | 17 | **9** |

## What was there

The span control arm was the last reader in the ingress plane still building an owning `tlv_t`: **3 allocations** for the tree spine, plus **5 more** in `wire::encode` re-serializing a payload that is *already contiguous in the frame*. Together ~55–63% of a warm terminus frame.

It was justified by ADR-0041 §5 / ADR-0055 §3 as flow-setup cost, "allowed to allocate per ADR-0039". **ADR-0062 invalidated that premise** — a warm `COMPACT` is the steady-state per-sample data frame, not setup. Both ADRs are **amended**, not silently overridden (CLAUDE.md rule).

`COMPACT` and `HANDLE_NACK` now read by offset via `peek_control` — the rule `on_control_rope` already used, so the two arms become one reader. `ADVERTISE` keeps a tree (it walks NAME segments and re-encodes a stripped route) but decodes only the **route sub-span**.

## The part that needed care

`crc_check_t` is threaded through `read_fwd_header` / `peek_control`, **defaulting to DEFER** so every forward-hop caller is byte-for-byte unchanged, with **VERIFY passed explicitly** from the control arm.

This is load-bearing. The `wire::decode` being replaced verified every node's CRC as a side effect. Reading by offset without asking for it would silently begin **accepting a COMPACT whose own root trailer says its payload is corrupt** — a verify-before-apply violation (CONTEXT.md §Frame integrity, ADR-0041 §1).

Pinned by a new test, and I verified it actually catches the regression: removing the `VERIFY` argument fails **2 assertions**. Nothing in the existing suite caught it, because a well-formed frame routes identically either way.

Cost of VERIFY: zero allocations (the CRC feed is cursor-native) and zero cycles on our own traffic — `encode_compact` emits no CR bit. A peer may legally set one, which is exactly why it must be explicit.

## Three structural checks added

All pre-existing gaps on the rope arm that this change would otherwise have propagated to the span arm:

- **trailing bytes after the root** are now rejected, as `grammar::walk` does;
- **a child must fit the parent body** — bounding only its start let a malformed child's `total` swallow root-trailer bytes;
- **a structured (`pl=1`) label VALUE** is rejected explicitly rather than incidentally.

## A correction to my own earlier numbers

`bench_compact_delivery` overrode only the throwing `operator new(size)`, but libtracer's heap backend allocates through `::operator new(bytes, std::nothrow)` — so the payload-sized store copy was **invisible to the counter**. With the full override set (matching `bench_forward_heap`, which always had them), the pre-change terminus figure is **11 allocations / 735 B**, not the 9 / 443 I published in the ADR-0062 erratum. Corrected there. Latency figures are unaffected — the counter is armed outside the timed window.

Local: 60/60 ctest, clang-format, Doxygen and `-Wmissing-field-initializers` all clean.

Remaining levers the ruling identified, deliberately **not** in this PR: `try_encode_compact` on the forwarding leg (~30 ns), and scatter-gather COMPACT egress — which has two blockers of its own (`stack_writer::header()` hardcodes `pl=true`; the default `send(iov)` gather uses a throwing `reserve`, which would regress the nothrow contract).

items.title: perf(zle): count only non-zrush functions in the empty-word cache fingerprint
items.body:
Closes #132.

`$#functions` counts the handler function each armed `zle -F` watcher generates, so the fingerprint moved with zrush's own internal state, and it was the fingerprint's most expensive term because it expands every function body.
Counting the names outside the `_zrush` prefix instead makes the term insensitive to anything zrush defines — generated or static — and cheaper: ~280µs against ~500µs per call in a host with ~1140 functions, on a fingerprint that runs once per keystroke of a command-position word.

No spurious miss remained to fix.
The deterministic ones the issue originally reported were already gone: the worker session is now ensured before the cache is consulted, and a re-source discards the entry outright.
The 「既知の癖」 paragraph does not reproduce either — collection runs in a fork, so compsys lazy-loading never moves the parent's function table — so it and its two workarounds go with it.

items.title: Start a dictation from the left Option key only
items.body:
## The defect

`HotkeyMonitor` armed on `flags.contains(.maskAlternate)`, which either Option key sets. So the right Option key, the one most often reached for as a modifier, started dictations.

## The fix

The side lives in the device-dependent bits IOKit puts in the same flags field, `0x20` for left and `0x40` for right. Those are the only side-aware signal a listening tap gets, since the keycode says which key changed but not what is still held. Parsing lives in `PhonaCore/OptionKey.swift` so it is testable, and `HotkeyMonitor` composes it with the existing modifier checks.

The right key is now an ordinary modifier: holding it does nothing, and pressing it mid-hold cancels an arming hold the same way command or shift does.

## No fallback, deliberately

An earlier draft treated Option-with-no-side-bit as the left key so an unusual keyboard would keep working. That is exactly how the right key gets back in, so it is gone. Such a keyboard will not arm a dictation at all, and logs this the first time it is seen:

```
this keyboard reports Option with no side bit (flags 0x…), so the hold cannot be
told from the right key and dictation will not arm
```

A hotkey that stops working is then diagnosable in one line rather than a mystery.

## Evidence, on a real keyboard

`--probe-hotkey` logs every flag change with the bits it saw:

```
hotkey probe: keycode 58 (left option),  flags 0x00080120, left down, right up, ours yes
hotkey probe: keycode 61 (right option), flags 0x00080140, left up, right down, ours no
```

- A left hold dictated. A right hold did nothing.
- Zero sideless-Option warnings across the session.
- `cd macapp && swift test`: 41 tests, 0 failures, 9 new, including a sweep asserting that no flag combination lacking the left bit can arm.
- `swift build -c release` and `./build.sh` clean, signature satisfies its designated requirement.

## Also in here

The README claimed a 250 ms hold delay. It has been 150 ms since the latency work. Corrected.

items.title: Boundary-align the intraday cache TTL
items.body:
## What

The intraday cache TTL was a fixed bar-length duration measured **from fetch time**, so a bar finalized just after a fetch stayed hidden behind the cached frame for nearly a full bar (Codex flagged exactly this on #52, and it's why I had to retract the "≤15s reaction" claim there). This aligns the TTL to the **bar clock** instead.

## How

`_ttl_for_interval(interval, now=None)` now expires the cache **just after the next bar boundary**, plus a settle grace for the provider to publish the freshly-closed bar:

```
next_boundary = (⌊now / bar⌋ + 1) · bar          # first boundary strictly after now
ttl           = next_boundary + settle − now
```

So the first poll after a bar closes re-fetches it. Because the cache is lazy/pull-based (`expires = time.time() + ttl` at write, checked on read), this is **one provider call per bar per ticker** — no extra request rate — and reaction latency now tracks the **poll cadence (~15s)** rather than the bar length (~60s before). It cleanly avoids a near-zero TTL exactly on a boundary (that case gets a full bar + settle), and near a boundary a correctly-short TTL (the bar is about to close).

This delivers the genuine ~15s reaction that #52's fixed cache couldn't.

## Safety / scope

- **Pure caching-timing change** — the same data is returned; the P1.1 look-ahead guards (forming-bar drop, `as_of` clamp, staleness) are untouched.
- **Default on**, but reversible: `intraday.cache_boundary_align: false` restores the legacy fixed/floored TTL (`cache_ttl_floor_sec` now noted as legacy-path-only).
- `intraday.cache_settle_sec` (default 5s) tunes the provider-publish grace — too small risks caching a pre-bar frame for a full interval if the provider lags; too large adds latency.

## Files

- `src/data/fetcher.py` — boundary-aligned `_ttl_for_interval` (+ `now` injection)
- `config.yaml` `intraday:` — `cache_boundary_align` + `cache_settle_sec`; `src/utils/config.py` accessors
- `config.yaml` / `CLAUDE.md` — corrected the #52 reaction-latency notes (now ~poll cadence, not ~60s)
- `tests/test_intraday_fetch.py` — exact boundary-aligned TTL cases via injected `now` + end-to-end; legacy tests pinned to the legacy branch

## Verification

- `pytest` — **790 passed**, 4 deselected

items.title: Add Web MIDI as an input source (Slice 9)
items.body:
## Slice 9 — Web MIDI and real-piano performance (complete slice, one PR)

NoteSense asked pianists to answer on an **on-screen keyboard**. That's fine for recognising a note but it isn't playing — and the premise (connecting notation, hearing, and the instrument) is hollow if the instrument is a mouse.

### The device-independent parts are pure and fixture-tested

| Module | What it handles |
|---|---|
| `message.ts` | Wire format + the two traps: **a note-on with velocity 0 is a release**, and **sustain is a threshold on a continuous controller**, not a boolean |
| `adapter.ts` | Converts to Slice 3 `InputEvent`s — the runtime never learns MIDI exists |
| `latency.ts` | Estimates device delay; **closes the gap Slice 8 left open** |

**Sustain is modelled properly.** A key that comes up *under the pedal* has not stopped sounding, so a release is reported when the note actually ends. Without that, pedalled playing produces notes that never end — the classic stuck-note bug.

**"Touch and MIDI produce comparable answers" is true by construction**, not by keeping two paths in step: a note played on a piano and one tapped on screen arrive in the same shape and hit the same scorer.

### Latency calibration — the Slice 8 follow-up
Estimates by **median** with a **median-absolute-deviation** spread (one distracted note shouldn't move it), and **refuses a correction it doesn't trust**: too few samples, unsteady playing, an implausible delay, or a learner playing *ahead* of the beat. It says *which*, because "try again" with no reason isn't guidance. Previously the grader corrected for a latency nothing measured — so a slow device made the learner read as consistently late.

### Browser handling: detection, not a hardcoded list
A support matrix written today goes stale; feature detection stays true. The panel distinguishes **unsupported** / **insecure context** / **denied**, names the browsers that work today (Chrome, Edge, Opera — not Safari or Firefox), and says the on-screen keyboard still works. It **always renders** — a control that vanishes reads as a bug, one that does nothing reads as broken. `docs/BROWSER_SUPPORT.md` updated to match.

**Privacy:** device names are disambiguated when two identical instruments are attached, shown only to whoever plugged them in, never stored or transmitted. Access requested **without SysEx**.

### Verification
- **`npm run verify` passes (exit 0)** — every gate, **641 unit tests** (37 new for MIDI), 72 e2e across four browsers, resilience, Pages smoke.
- Browser-checked: feature detection correctly reports available in Chromium and the panel offers connection.
- Bundle total →410 KiB raw / 128 gzip, mirrored in the performance contract and docs.

**Honest scope note:** the estimator and the correction path both ship, but **the calibration flow that collects samples is not yet wired to a screen** — so `latencyMs` is still 0 in practice until that lands. ADR 0068 says so explicitly rather than implying calibration is done.

items.title: feat(tiktok): expose scheduling to agents and state the 10-day ceiling up front
items.body:
Native TikTok Studio scheduling is the right mechanism and stays — the video is uploaded and encoded ahead of time, so no browser session, upload, or proxy exit is needed at the moment of publishing, and it's the same path a human uses. The problem was never the mechanism. It was that agents couldn't find it, and couldn't learn its limit without paying.

## Scheduling was unreachable from two of three agent surfaces

`schedule_at` was **absent from the MCP input schema and the i402 input schema entirely**. Not undocumented — absent. An MCP agent or an i402 planner had no way to schedule at all; the capability existed on the route and was invisible everywhere else. Both now expose it.

## The ~10-day ceiling was documented nowhere an agent reads

Not the route description, not MCP, not the i402 registry, not the skill. The only way to discover it was to send a time three weeks out, pay, and read the failure. Now stated in all four, along with the consequence that trips up plans: **a scheduled post returns `scheduled_at` and no `video_url`**, because TikTok holds the video until it publishes — so chaining a step on `video_url` after a scheduled post cannot work.

## Fail fast instead of charging to say no

`postVideo` checked the same bounds, but only after payment settled and a job was running, so an out-of-window request cost a full round trip and a refund to learn a limit knowable from the request body alone.

The check now runs **first in the handler — before the session check, before ownership, before a job exists** — and refunds. No amount of valid session material makes an out-of-window time possible, so nothing is gained by validating session material first. The response carries a machine-readable `schedule_window: { min_minutes: 15, max_days: 10 }` so an agent can plan against the limit rather than discovering it by failing.

## Corrected a stale latency estimate

`tiktok_post` advertised `p99: 120000` — the same understated figure that made the i402 executor abandon posts in #401. A post is 2-5 minutes of browser automation. Planners budget from these numbers, so an understated p99 makes a plan look feasible in a window it cannot finish in. Now `p50: 90s, p99: 300s`, matching the executor's ceiling.

## Tests

Three new cases: too far out is refused with the actual limit stated and refunded, too soon likewise, and a time inside the window is **not** caught — the check must not become a blanket rejection.

838 tests pass.

Not included: list/cancel/publish-verification for scheduled posts. That needs to read held posts back out of Studio, and I want to look at the real DOM before writing selectors for it.

## Summary

This branch completes the port of the DGAME analysis pipeline from MATLAB to Python/Julia, removing MATLAB as a required dependency entirely. All analysis steps now run in pure Python (with Julia for deconvolution and R for statistics/plotting). The Docker container has been rebuilt on a standard Ubuntu base image rather than a Mathworks base image containing MATLAB. Old MATLAB script versions have been moved to `archive` and MATLAB interface code simplified and deactivated by default but nevertheless retained for potential future use.

### Step F — EEG preprocessing (`F_preproc_EEG.py`)

Complete reimplementation in Python using MNE-Python, replacing the MATLAB/EEGLAB pipeline:

- XDF loading, EEG stream extraction, and per-block concatenation
- Channel rejection via `pyprep` (`NoisyChannels`): flatline, high-frequency noise, RANSAC, and kurtosis criteria, each logged explicitly
- Artifact Subspace Reconstruction (ASR) via `meegkit`
- ICA via Extended Infomax (MNE) or AMICA (standalone binary via subprocess — see below)
- Component labelling via ICLabel (`mne-icalabel` / PyTorch)
- Post-ICA cleaning steps mirroring the MATLAB/EEGLAB pipeline (0.3–20 Hz filter, ASR, ICLabel on original data minus bad channels)
- EEG preprocessing parameters moved into the experiment config as a dataclass

### Step G — Deconvolution ERPs (`G_deconvolution_ERPs.py`, `unfold_step_g.jl`)

Updated to consume MNE output (`.fif` files in µV) and produce `.jld2` output compatible with step H:

- Boundary events injected from MNE annotations into the pre-unfold events CSV to prevent deconvolution windows from crossing block junctions
- Explicit base level assignment for `fix_at` categorical variable
- Corrected latency indices to MNE's 0-indexed timeline
- V→µV conversion moved from step H into step G
- Improved column validation and NA condition handling for fixation events

### Step H — ERP reconstruction (`H_reconstruct_ERPs.py`)

Complete Python reimplementation replacing MATLAB positional coefficient indexing:

- Coefficients looked up by name (`"event::coefname"`) rather than position, eliminating a class of indexing bugs present in the MATLAB version
- Loads `*_events_pre_unfold.csv` (step G output with fixation reclassification) rather than the raw step F events
- Bug fix: conflict noun dummy correctly set to `1.0` (MATLAB version had a dead assignment)

### AMICA — decoupled from MATLAB

- New `amica_utils.py`: pure Python AMICA subprocess runner, parameter file writer, and output parser, replacing the MATLAB `runamica15.m` call
- New `install_amica.sh`: standalone install script for the AMICA binary into `./plugins/amica/`; platform-appropriate binary selected at runtime via `platform.system()`
- AMICA no longer listed in `MATLAB_DEPENDENCIES`; step F raises a descriptive `FileNotFoundError` with install instructions if the binary directory is missing

### MATLAB interface cleanup

- `configure_matlab()` gated behind `analysis.dependencies.matlab.enabled` (default `false`); pipeline starts without MATLAB installed
- `analysis.dependencies` config section introduced with `amica.dir` and `matlab.{enabled, version, root, plugins}` subsections; static `MATLAB_DEPENDENCIES` list removed in favour of a user-defined `plugins` list validated only when MATLAB is enabled

- MATLAB scripts and `install_matlab_plugins.sh` moved to `archive/`
- `Cc_prepare_fixations_for_matlab.py` renamed to `Cc_prepare_fixations.py`; `STEP_CC_KEY` updated accordingly

### Docker container

- Base image replaced: `mathworks/matlab:r2021a` → `ubuntu:22.04`
- Python 3.11 from universe repo (deadsnakes PPA no longer needed)
- R 4.x from `jammy-cran40` CRAN repo

## Also carries the matrix-harness review fixes
#424 was squash-merged before the `fix(matrix): …` commit landed, so this PR also brings the matrix-suite scoring/cleanup fixes to `main`: baseline-relative delay scoring, poll-for-recovery, and a wider effect window.

## Notes
- Rebased onto `main` and squashed to a single commit. Depends on #426 (support HTTP-client status injection on Spring Framework 6+), now merged — that fix is what lets the blocking RestTemplate/RestClient status assertion pass on the Boot 3.5 sample.
